en: He who is the sole kinsman of the world, the remover of death, birth, old age, sickness, and sorrow;
he who is the slayer of the afflictions for those in the realms of gods, humans, hell-beings, pretas, and animals;
and he who is the constant bestower of the supreme nectar of tranquility, wisdom, and bliss.
I bow to that Lord of Sages, whose feet are rubbed by the hollows of the edges of the crowns of the gods;
through ignorance of whom this world— established among gods, humans, hell-beings, pretas, and animals— wanders incessantly like a wheel produced by the labor of a potter.
Unshakable and changeless, like a mountain against the wing-winds of a swarm of locusts;

a fertile field for the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) that yields abundant fruit, and a wish-fulfilling tree (*vāsava-vṛkṣa*) for all virtues—I bow to that noble Saṅgha, [who acts] according to the words of the One Possessing Ten Powers. 23.1.3
Though addressed as a "śramaṇa" by the world, and though professing the state of a śramaṇa within himself,
he who has cast away the mind of a śramaṇa— [even such a one is not a true śramaṇa].
He who has gone forth but whose passion for desire has not gone forth, who wears the saffron robe yet is not free from impurity— he is indeed like a hawk in the body of a cuckoo and must be avoided.
He carries the bowl by virtue of his qualities, yet he is not a worthy recipient even while bearing the insignia; he is neither a householder nor a mendicant. (Saundarananda 7.49)
Like a cloud without water, like a pit that has run dry, like a crop that has perished, or like a seed that does not sprout—
the Sugata spoke thus to the monk who had fallen away from the conduct of a monk.
Like a lamp in a painting, he both exists and does not exist—
he who possesses sense-faculties, feet, and arms, and who is endowed with consciousness.
He lives by begging and does not remain engaged in worldly affairs;
he should indeed be known as one whose true nature is concealed by the banner of dharma, like a snake dwelling within its excellent slough. (23.1.7)
Delighting in proper conduct and the sphere of activity, pure in virtue and with senses subdued, he wanders without attachment toward sense objects;
he is constantly at odds with faults as if they were enemies.
He should be known as liberated, even if he is a householder—
[he] whose mind is embraced by tranquility and remains under control,
and who perceives the world as unsubstantial and empty.
He should be called a "śramaṇa," for he makes known his outward mark according to its true meaning; he enjoys almsfood according to the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Having caused them to travel upon the noble path—auspicious, fearless, and sublime—
He who has attained the ageless, unassailable, and imperishable state—
the seer spoke of that ascetic as he truly is; he who is endowed with the specific fruits of asceticism is designated as one who has accomplished his purpose.

He who is liberated and free from fever, or he who dwells within the body or the afflictions yet remains possessed of afflictions while striving for the destruction of existence, or he who is a practitioner endowed with virtue— he alone is to be known as a *śramaṇa*; but he who is unsteady and does not abide in the Dharma is not.
"Even though he dwells in the marks [of a monk], he is devoid of virtues; such a person does not deserve to be addressed as a *śramaṇa*.
Therefore, casting aside your childishness, always remain eager to hear the words of the Jina."
Both of these are exceedingly difficult to obtain:
the word of the Victor and birth as a human being.
(Samādhirāja Prologue, Ms. A, v. 40)
§1 Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:

§2 "Monks, there are these five disadvantages in a charnel ground. What are the five? It is impure, foul-smelling, terrifying, abounding in predatory yakṣas, and it causes much lamentation among the people. In the same way, monks, there are these five disadvantages in a person who is like a charnel ground. What are the five?"

§2.1 Here, a person is possessed of impure bodily action, and is possessed of impure verbal and mental action. Just as a charnel ground is impure, so do I describe that person; this is the first disadvantage in a person who is like a charnel ground.

Furthermore, for that person who is possessed of impure bodily action, and possessed of impure vocal and mental action, an evil reputation, disrepute, and ill-famed report arise in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Just as a charnel ground is foul-smelling, so, I say, is that person; this is the second disadvantage regarding a person who is like a charnel ground.

Furthermore, wise fellow-practitioners avoid from afar one who is possessed of impure bodily action, impure vocal action, and impure mental action. Just as a charnel ground is full of terror, so do I describe that person; this is the third disadvantage regarding a person who is like a charnel ground.

§2.4 Furthermore, individuals of a similar nature associate with, frequent, and attend upon that person who is possessed of impure bodily action, impure vocal action, and impure mental action. Just as one would approach a charnel ground abounding in predatory yakṣas, I say that such a person is comparable to that; this is the fourth disadvantage regarding a person comparable to a charnel ground.

Furthermore, having seen him—endowed with impure bodily action, endowed with impure vocal action, and endowed with impure mental action—whether in a village or in the forest, wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life say: "This venerable one is an actor of such deeds and a speaker of such words; he is an impure thorn to the village. Just as a charnel ground causes lamentation for many people, so do I describe that person. This is the fifth disadvantage regarding a person who is like a charnel ground.
Thus spoke the Blessed One; with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.

But for one who possesses neither a heart as firm as adamant nor pure moral conduct, there is neither a future world nor the fruit of karma. A widow, at least, protects her virtue out of fear of scandal to the family. (23.3.1)
Surely even a monk must especially protect the lineage of the Buddha.

(23.3.2) One whose ears and nose have been cut off feels no satisfaction upon seeing his reflection in a mirror; one whose conduct has become depleted and defiled does not wish to hear talk of virtuous discipline. (23.3.3)
For even if a monk of immoral conduct should have no fierce fear of the miserable realms,
the suffering caused by contempt right here in this world is already sufficient.
(23.3.4) If there is no stainless morality, then even very extensive learning becomes useless.
For without a boat, a staff does not carry a man across the great ocean. Likewise,
although Śākyamuni was standing nearby, he was not seen by him who had not diligently observed the precepts of the Blessed One.
For even though the Blessed One has passed into final nirvāṇa, he is seen as if present by that teacher who,
with effort, guards the training as he would his own life;
the virtuous one becomes trustworthy on earth, like a sage to those seeking protection.
And even when the time of death has arrived, he does not fall into terror;

surrounded in heaven by hosts of apsarases, he is served with ease by the winds of the Mandākinī, which are fragrant with the scent of golden lotuses and most beautiful with their praiseworthy qualities.

Milk contained in a vessel does not bring such satisfaction to a calf as that which it receives from the mother’s udder while it drinks with its head raised and moving. (23.3.9) *Jaina Daśavaikālikasūtra 5/5.15*
In the same way, milk consisting of well-spoken words, when placed in a vessel of immoral character,
does not produce such satisfaction as it does when it has fallen from the mouth of one possessed of virtue.
(23.3.10) — *Jaina Daśavaikālikasūtra* 5/5.16.
Just as fire located in a cremation ground is not resorted to even when one seeks warmth despite effort,
so too the speech of one who has fallen from moral conduct is not accepted, even if it is beneficial. 23.3.11 (Jaina *Daśavaikālikasūtra* 5/5.17)

Even if he is learned, one who is devoid of right conduct is not relied upon by the virtuous, just as a well belonging to a *caṇḍāla*, though filled with cool water, is not used by those of noble birth. (23.3.12)
For those devoid of practice, affliction is not pacified by mere learning alone.
For the disease of a sick person does not subside merely by hearing of the medicine; like old trees with withered leaves, [they fall away].
Like clusters of lotuses consumed by frost,
men who have fallen from their moral conduct do not shine,
like kings who have been deprived of their kingdom.
What is the use of your vast lineage, which is ultimately meaningless?
Rely upon ethical discipline; it is the preeminent lineage of ascetics.
Indeed, without ethical discipline, even a vast lineage does not shine.
For a family is indeed ruined by a defect in conduct, just as what is the use of the thundering of a waterless cloud,
or the pride of a man devoid of virtue?
What is the use of armor for one who is cowardly in battles?
What is the use of a hermitage for one who is deluded and devoid of virtue?
What is the use of even extensive sacred learning for one who is bereft of right conduct?
With various kinds of weapons, as if in a great battle against a coward;
whatever is the difference between the ocean and a cow’s footprint,
that indeed is the difference between generosity and virtuous conduct.
If someone were to give gifts with a joyful mind for a hundred years,
one who would observe ethical discipline for even a single day excels over that person. (23.3.19)
Even by a butcher or even by a caṇḍāla, giving can be practiced; but by no one whatsoever is ethical discipline (śīla) able to be maintained. 23.3.20
Through generosity, one obtains enjoyments wherever one is reborn.
Through ethical discipline, one attains wealth, heaven, and even nirvāṇa. Even if one is prosperous, one is not a great master of giving merely by means of bestowing gifts.
But through pure ethical discipline, one is remembered as a great lord of generosity. Now, who shall surpass him in the timely giving of the gift at the right moment?

But by means of pure morality, all of that is indeed conquered: as long as Mount Meru, the abode of the gods, made of gold with peaks of jewels, stands high with its broad summits where the groves have been enjoyed by the wives of the foremost deities; ||| 23.3.23 ||| [as long as it stands, so long does one conquer through pure morality.]
May this stainless jewel of the Sugata’s word, thick and skilled in pacifying the afflictions, first dispel the darkness residing within the mental continuum of sentient beings.
"Whatever beings are here... (23.3.25)
